translationScientificConditionBaseline.mustPreserve: With a fixed source-charge distribution, electrostatic-force work depends only on endpoints and is zero around a closed path. Energy conservation alone does not make arbitrary time-varying electric fields conservative. A is work of the electric force only, equal to minus the potential-energy change using a shared reference zero. Prior equation (8-22) is restricted to its uniform-field distance model.

Choose a common potential-energy zero; a sufficiently small test charge must not alter the original source distribution. Interaction potential energy at a fixed point is proportional to signed, nonzero q. Potential is E_P/q, independent of test-charge choice, in both uniform and other electrostatic fields. Unit-positive-charge potential energy is an interpretation, not kinetic or total energy divided by charge.
Electric field intensity is a force-describing vector including direction; potential U is an energy-describing scalar which fixes potential energy only given the charge and selected reference.

Use the two-parallel-plate uniform-field model, neglect edges, choose the negative plate as the potential-energy and potential zero, measure distance normally toward the positive plate, and use field magnitude, so U=Ed holds only in that region.

Changing the arbitrary zero adds the same constant to every potential. Values can describe and compare after reference choice; the change between two points is reference-independent and directly relates to electrostatic work.

E_P=qU applies for the same moving charge. Retain the unnumbered initial E_P in the source equation (8-25) and explicitly explain that it is the starting potential energy; E_{P_2} is the ending energy. Both signed q and the potential change determine the work sign, including negative charges.

Potential change is final minus initial, Delta U=U_2-U_1. This lesson instead defines potential difference / voltage in initial-minus-final order V=U_1-U_2=-Delta U for the same endpoints. Reversing endpoints reverses voltage sign.

The current/lighting example concerns a circuit section treatable electrostatically, not arbitrary total work with induction. Voltage equals electric-force work divided by the signed nonzero charge for the specified direction. Fixed sources and negligible test-charge disturbance remain conditions; exclude work of other forces, power-source internal forces, and induced closed-circuit work.
Potential-difference units follow work/charge. In SI, positive 1 coulomb moving initial-to-final with +1 joule electric-force work gives +1 joule/coulomb in that order, called the volt.

The original also uses historical electrostatic units: moving one positive electrostatic charge unit with one erg of electric-force work defines its potential-difference unit. Do not mix unconverted SI/historical values. Preserve the source approximate conversion and its explicit non-exactness. Literal unit names may be translated through the native math_signature contract without altering operators, numbers, charge units, or potential-difference units.
